> **What this case shows** — walking *feels* rhythmic; nonlinear dynamics lets you
> **measure** it. On real ankle accelerometry, **recurrence quantification** and
> **approximate/sample entropy** separate rhythmic locomotion from aperiodic
> activity: **walking** is highly deterministic and regular (RQA determinism
> **0.921**, approximate entropy **0.455**), **running** even more so (determinism
> **0.983**), while aperiodic **ironing** is neither (determinism **0.382**,
> approximate entropy **1.280**) — a **0.54** determinism gap and a **0.83**
> entropy gap between walking and ironing. **How to read it** — left, walking's
> repeating stride spikes; centre, ironing's structureless trace; right,
> determinism high / entropy low exactly for the rhythmic activities.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — reconstruct the attractor by **delay embedding**, then read
**recurrence determinism / laminarity** (how much the trajectory repeats) and
**approximate / sample entropy** (how predictable the next sample is) — the
regularity of the movement.
**Way of thinking** — rhythm is *recurrence*: a periodic movement revisits nearby
states, so its recurrence plot fills with diagonal lines (high determinism) and
its entropy is low. Hold the embedding and threshold **fixed** across conditions so
the comparison is fair.
**Ecosystem usage** — `recurrenceQuantification()`, `approximateEntropy()`,
`sampleEntropy()` (PhysioMoCap) on any signal; `maxLyapunovExponent()` and
`floquetMultipliers()` complete the nonlinear-stability toolkit.
:::

## Proposition

Recurrence quantification and entropy separate rhythmic locomotion from aperiodic
activity on real accelerometry: walking is deterministic and regular (DET 0.921,
ApEn 0.455), running more so (DET 0.983), ironing neither (DET 0.382, ApEn 1.280).

## Question & goal

**The question is about the *character* of the dynamics, not its amount.** Two
signals can have the same variance yet be worlds apart — one a clean rhythm, the
other noise. Gait is a quasi-periodic limit cycle; its regularity is a motor-control
marker (it drops in ageing and neurological disease). We ask whether recurrence and
entropy measures, on a plain ankle accelerometer, capture that rhythmic determinism
and tell it apart from an aperiodic activity.

## Challenge & approach

We take the ankle-acceleration magnitude for one subject across four activities,
delay-embed each (m = 4, τ = 8, fixed), and compute the **recurrence determinism
and laminarity**, the **approximate entropy** and the **sample entropy**. The
embedding and recurrence threshold are held fixed so the numbers are comparable.

## Data

**PAMAP2** (Reiss & Stricker, UCI #231) — subject 101, ankle accelerometer at
100 Hz, walking / running / vacuuming / ironing. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Walking's ankle-acceleration magnitude repeats stride by stride (left); ironing
is structureless (centre); recurrence determinism is high and entropy low exactly
for the rhythmic activities (right).](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* the stride spikes on the left recur at a steady period — that
recurrence is what drives the high determinism. Ironing (centre) has no such
rhythm, so its determinism collapses and its entropy jumps.

| activity | RQA determinism | approx entropy | sample entropy |
|---|---|---|---|
| running | **0.983** | 0.577 | 0.034 |
| walking | **0.921** | **0.455** | 0.035 |
| vacuuming | 0.734 | 0.450 | 0.074 |
| ironing | **0.382** | **1.280** | 2.434 |

## Conclusion

On real accelerometry the nonlinear measures do exactly what they should: rank
rhythmic locomotion as deterministic and regular, and aperiodic activity as neither.
The transferable takeaway: **rhythm is recurrence — quantify it with determinism
and entropy (holding the embedding fixed), and you have an objective handle on
gait regularity, a marker that degrades with age and disease.**

## Open questions

- **Orbital stability** of the gait limit cycle (`floquetMultipliers()`) and
  **long-range stride-interval correlations** (DFA) are complementary markers that
  need segmented multi-stride kinematics or a stride-time series, not a raw
  accelerometer window. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| step | function | package |
|---|---|---|
| recurrence determinism / laminarity | `recurrenceQuantification()` | PhysioMoCap |
| approximate entropy (regularity) | `approximateEntropy()` | PhysioMoCap |
| sample entropy (regularity, less biased) | `sampleEntropy()` | PhysioMoCap |
| local dynamic stability | `maxLyapunovExponent()` | PhysioMoCap |
| orbital stability (multi-stride) | `floquetMultipliers()` | PhysioMoCap |

**Choosing the parameters:** pick the embedding (`m`, `tau`) once — from an
average-mutual-information / false-nearest-neighbours check — and reuse it across
all conditions; fix the recurrence threshold via a target recurrence rate so
determinism is comparable. Higher determinism / lower entropy = more regular rhythm.

```r
library(PhysioMoCap)
rq <- recurrenceQuantification(ankle_acc, m = 4, tau = 8, target_rr = 0.1)
rq$DET; approximateEntropy(ankle_acc); sampleEntropy(ankle_acc)
```
